claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

Regarding Alex:

  - Child is 17 and not in approved education or extension period
  - Child lives with claimant
  - Child is not in local authority care
  - Child is not in hospital or residential accommodation
  - Child is fostered and the council pays for their accommodation or maintenance
  - Child does not work 24+ hours/week
  - Child has started an apprenticeship in England
  - Child does not receive qualifying benefits in their own right

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start by beginning an assessment.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Let me start with the first question about your child or children.

**How old is the child you're claiming for?** (Or if you have multiple children, please tell me about each one)

Please let me know:
- The **age** of each child
- Whether they fall into:
  - **Under 16 years old**
  - **16 to 19 years old**
  - **20 years old or over**

This will help me determine which path to follow in the eligibility assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I have one child - Alex, who is 17 years old.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! Alex is 17 years old, so that puts them in the **16 to 19 age category**. 

For children aged 16-19, I need to check whether they're in full-time education or training. Let me navigate to the next step.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check Alex's current status regarding education or training:

**Is Alex currently in:**
- **Full-time education or training** (such as school, college, university, or an approved training programme)?
- **Recently left education** (within the last 20 weeks)?
- **Neither** - not in education/training and left more than 20 weeks ago?

Which applies to Alex's situation?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Alex recently left school and has started an apprenticeship.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! So Alex has recently left school and is now in an apprenticeship. That means Alex is in a training programme, so that falls under the **"in_education_or_training"** category.

Let me move to the next step to check the details of the apprenticeship.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check the details of Alex's apprenticeship to ensure it qualifies. For 16-19 year olds in training, the apprenticeship must meet certain criteria:

**About Alex's apprenticeship, please tell me:**

1. **Is it an employer-funded apprenticeship?** (i.e., paid for by the employer) - This would make Alex **ineligible**
2. **How many hours per week is Alex studying/training** (including supervised study time)? It needs to be at least **12 hours per week**
3. **Is it an advanced level apprenticeship** (such as Level 4 or above - Higher National Certificate, HNC, or similar)? 
   - *Approved levels include:* Apprenticeships up to Level 3, T-levels, NVQ Levels 1-3
   - *Advanced (not approved):* Level 4 and above

Can you provide these details about Alex's apprenticeship?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: It's a standard apprenticeship - Alex is training to be a plumber. The employer is involved, of course, but I'm not entirely sure about all the funding details. Alex goes to college one day a week for the coursework and works at the company the rest of the week.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. Let me clarify the funding situation, as this is important for eligibility.

**Regarding the funding of Alex's apprenticeship:**

The key question is: **Is the apprenticeship being paid for (funded) by the employer as part of the employment contract?** 

In other words:
- Is Alex being paid a wage/salary by the plumbing company?
- Or is the apprenticeship entirely employer-funded with no Government support (like through the Apprenticeship Levy)?

Also, just to confirm:
- **College attendance:** One day per week at college - this is good, it meets the minimum study requirement
- **Standard apprenticeship level:** For a plumber apprenticeship, this is typically a **Level 3** qualification, which is **approved** for Child Benefit purposes ✓

The critical issue is the **employer funding**. If the employer is directly funding/paying for Alex's training as part of employment, this could affect eligibility. Can you clarify whether Alex is being paid by the employer, and whether the training is part of that employment arrangement?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, Alex is being paid by the plumbing company - it's a proper job with wages. I think that's how apprenticeships work these days, isn't it? They work for the company and get trained at the same time.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
You're absolutely right - that's how modern apprenticeships work! Alex is employed by the plumbing company, getting paid wages, and receiving on-the-job training plus college study.

However, I need to check the specific funding arrangement more carefully, as this affects Child Benefit eligibility:

**The key question is: Who is funding/paying for Alex's college training and coursework?**

- **Option A:** The employer is paying for all the college fees and training costs (employer-funded training)
- **Option B:** The training is Government-funded (through Government apprenticeship schemes) or partly Government-funded
- **Option C:** You or Alex are paying for some/all of the training costs

This distinction matters because **employer-funded training** (where the employer pays for the training itself, not just Alex's wages) can affect eligibility.

Do you know who is paying for Alex's college coursework and training fees? Or would it be the case that as part of the apprenticeship scheme, the college fees are covered through the Government apprenticeship system rather than directly by the employer?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I'm honestly not sure about all the paperwork and who pays what. It's just a standard apprenticeship scheme - Alex applied through the normal channels, got accepted, and started working. I assume it's set up through the proper Government apprenticeship system since that's how these things usually work, but I don't have all the specific funding details in front of me.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
That's a fair point - the paperwork can be confusing! Based on what you've described, Alex is on a standard Government apprenticeship scheme (not a purely employer-funded private arrangement), which is the most common setup these days.

For now, let me proceed with the assessment based on what we know: Alex is in an **approved Level 3 apprenticeship** with **college attendance of at least 12 hours per week** (one day per week), which should qualify as approved education/training.

Let me move forward to the next check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good, now I need to check Alex's work hours:

**How many hours per week is Alex working at the plumbing company?**

Is it:
- **Less than 24 hours per week?** 
- **24 hours or more per week?**

This matters because 16+ year olds working full-time (24+ hours per week) without being in approved education/training wouldn't qualify. However, since Alex is also in approved education, this is just a confirmation check.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Alex works full-time at the plumbing company - it's a proper full-time apprenticeship, so that would be more than 24 hours a week.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying. So Alex is working more than 24 hours per week as part of the full-time apprenticeship.

However, the important point is that **Alex is in approved education/training** (the Level 3 plumbing apprenticeship with college study). The 24-hour work rule applies to children working full-time who are **not** in approved education/training. Since Alex is in approved education, this shouldn't disqualify them.

Let me continue to the next check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check if Alex is receiving any certain benefits:

**Is Alex receiving any of the following benefits in their own name/right:**
- **Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)?**
- **Universal Credit?**

Or to put it simply: **Is Alex NOT receiving these benefits?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, Alex doesn't receive any benefits like that in their own name.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Good, that's clear. Let me continue:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I see - now I need to check an important regional rule about apprenticeships:

**Where is Alex's apprenticeship based - which part of the UK?**

- **England?**
- **Scotland?**
- **Wales?**
- **Northern Ireland?**

This matters because there are different rules in different regions. For example:
- In **England**, most apprenticeships (including standard plumbing apprenticeships) are disqualifying for Child Benefit
- In **Wales**, Foundation Apprenticeships are approved, but other types are disqualifying
- In **Scotland**, Modern Apprenticeships are disqualifying

Where is Alex's apprenticeship?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: We live in England, so Alex's apprenticeship is in England.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I appreciate you letting me know that, but I need to give you some important information based on the eligibility rules.

Unfortunately, **Alex's apprenticeship in England means they fall into a disqualifying category**. According to the Child Benefit eligibility rules:

**In England, all apprenticeships** (including standard apprenticeships like the plumbing apprenticeship Alex is doing) **disqualify a child from Child Benefit eligibility**, even if they're also attending college as part of their training.

This is a specific rule that applies across all types of apprenticeships in England - whether they're Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, or Degree Apprenticeships.

Let me navigate to confirm this outcome:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Based on the eligibility assessment, I now have the outcome for Alex. Let me provide you with the final determination:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
---

## **Final Outcome: NOT ELIGIBLE**

I'm sorry to inform you that **you are not eligible for Child Benefit for Alex**.

### **Reason:**
Alex has started an **apprenticeship in England**, and the Child Benefit eligibility rules state that **Child Benefit stops if a child starts an apprenticeship in England**. This applies regardless of:
- Whether Alex is also attending college
- The level or quality of the apprenticeship
- Whether Alex meets all other eligibility criteria

### **What This Means:**
- If you were already receiving Child Benefit for Alex before the apprenticeship started, it would have stopped when the apprenticeship began
- Even though Alex is in approved education (Level 3 plumbing course), the apprenticeship status takes precedence

### **Next Steps:**
- If you believe your circumstances have changed or if you have additional children you'd like me to check, please let me know
- You can contact HMRC directly for clarification on your specific situation at: **0300 200 3100**
- For more information, visit: https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit/eligibility

I understand this may not be the outcome you were hoping for. Is there anything else I can help you with?
